          Pursuant to Sections 203(a)(1) and 203(a)(2) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) 1 and Part

33 of the Rules and Regulations of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or

“Commission”), 2 AEP Generation Resources Inc. (“GenResources” or the “Buyer”) and Longview

Power, LLC (“Longview”) (referred to collectively with GenResources as the “Applicants”)

respectfully request in this application (the “Application”) that the Commission authorize the

following transaction (“Proposed Transaction”) in which Mountain State Energy Holdings, LLC

(the “Seller”) will sell to GenResources 100% of the equity interests in Longview, which owns the

approximately 710 MW (summer rating) coal-fired generating facility located in Maidsville, West

Virginia (the “Facility”), so that Longview will become a direct subsidiary of the Buyer. 3

III.       THE PROPOSED TRANSACTION IS CONSISTENT WITH THE PUBLIC
           INTEREST

           Section 203(a)(4) of the FPA provides that the Commission must authorize a proposed

transaction under Section 203 if it determines that the transaction “will be consistent with the

public interest” and “will not result in cross-subsidization of a non-utility associate company or

the pledge or encumbrance of utility assets for the benefit of an associate company.” 13 The

Commission reviews three factors when evaluating a proposed transaction under the Section 203

public interest standard: (i) the effect on competition; (ii) the effect on rates; and (iii) the effect on

regulation. 14 As demonstrated below, the Proposed Transaction is consistent with the public

interest and will not raise any cross-subsidization concerns under the Commission’s applicable

precedent and otherwise meets the statutory requirements of Section 203 of the FPA.

           A.       The Proposed Transaction Will Not Have an Adverse Effect on Competition.

           When considering impacts on competition, the Commission reviews both horizontal

market power effects that may result from any increases in concentration in energy and capacity

markets are presumed to have no anti-competitive impact, regardless of the HHI change. See Merger Policy Statement

concentrated” markets, and transactions in such markets that increase the HHI by 50 points or fewer are unlikely to
have a significant anti-competitive impact, while transactions that increase the HHI by more than 100 points are
considered likely to reduce market competitiveness. See id.

         D.       The Proposed Transaction Will Not Result in Cross-Subsidization or the
                  Pledge or Encumbrance of Utility Assets.

         Under Section 203(a)(4) of the FPA and Section 2.26(f) of its regulations, 36 the

Commission considers whether a proposed transaction will result in a cross-subsidization of a non-

utility associate company by a utility company or in a pledge or encumbrance of utility assets for

the benefit of an associate company. 37 The Commission’s primary concern with respect to cross-

subsidization is whether a proposed transaction will result in a traditional utility with captive

customers cross-subsidizing an associate company to the harm of captive ratepayers. 38 Here, the

Proposed Transaction falls within one of the Commission’s “safe harbors” under Section

203(a)(4), such that detailed explanation and evidentiary support to demonstrate a lack of cross-

subsidization is not required. 39 As explained in Sections II and III above and set forth in Exhibit

M, the Proposed Transaction does not involve any franchised public utility with captive customers

(i.e., wholesale or retail electric energy customers served under cost-based regulation). The

FRAMEWORK FOR THE ANALYSIS

          Market power is defined as the ability of a firm to profitably maintain prices above
competitive levels for a significant period of time. Market power analysis of a proposed merger
or transaction that involves the combination of assets examines whether such transaction would
cause a material increase in market power or a significant reduction in the competitiveness of
relevant markets. The focus is on the horizontal effects of the transaction in those business areas
in which the combining firms are competitors. In most instances, a transaction will not affect
competition in markets in which the combining firms do not compete. The focus is properly on
those markets in which these entities or generating assets are actual or potential competitors. Of
relevance to our analysis, the Proposed Transaction will combine the generation affiliated with
AEP in PJM with the generation being acquired from Seller. The analysis is intended to measure
the adverse impact, if any, of the elimination of a competitor as a result of the combination in
relevant markets.

          Potential vertical market effects of a proposed merger or other combination relate to the
combining firms’ ability and incentives to use their market position over a product or service to
affect competition in a related business or market. For example, vertical effects could result if a
transaction created an opportunity and incentive to operate electric transmission facilities in a
manner that creates market power for the post-transaction company that did not exist previously.

                                   Data and Methods for DPT

          This exhibit describes data and assumptions used in the delivered price test (“DPT”)
study (“study”). Because the data are voluminous, we provide them in electronic workpapers.
This exhibit has six sections. Section I discusses the study’s representative periods. Section II
discusses the geographic regions and balancing authority areas. Section III discusses
generation resources, including adjustments to generating capacity for seasons, maintenance,
water availability, and long-term contracts. Section IV discusses the load data. Section V
discusses transmission, including transmission pricing and losses. Section VI discusses market
prices.

I. Time Periods

          The study calculates market shares and concentration indexes for electric energy for
ten representative periods during the year consistent with the Commission’s requirements. 1
The year is divided into three seasons (spring/fall, summer and winter), and each season is
divided into three or four periods based on NERC on-peak/off-peak definition and peak load
levels. The seasons are Spring/Fall, Summer, and Winter. For Spring/Fall and Winter, the
market conditions correspond to (1) the Top 10% of on-peak load hours for the season, (2) the
remaining on-peak load hours, and (3) off-peak hours. For Summer, the Top 1% of on-peak
load hours also are considered as a separate period for analysis. Each calculation of market
shares and concentration indexes reflects average conditions (e.g., average loads) during one
of the resulting ten periods during the year (e.g., Summer Peak). 2

III. Generation Resources

A. Generation Capacity and Ownership

       The study includes generating units located in the geographic region that are connected
to the power grid.

                 1.       Generating Unit Data

       The study uses data for summer and winter capability at the unit level reported in the
proprietary Hitachi Velocity Suite Generation Unit Capacity database. 4 The units include all
generation with a status of operating, standby, cold standby, restart, testing, or under
construction that will be online before December 31, 2027 and with a retirement date after
December 31, 2020 (for consideration of whether to include such generation in the analysis).
Generation units online on December 31, 2023 are used in the base price simulations for the
years 2023-2024. For the forward price simulations and the DPT calculations, the inclusion
of plants varies by season. For the Spring/Fall and Summer season, the inclusion cut-off date
is July 15, 2027. This is the date at which if a unit was online before or retired after this date
the unit was, on average, operating during the season. The cut-off date for the Winter season
is January 15, 2027. Hence, the study represents, on average, the period from December 2026
through November 2027.

                4.      Adjustments to Generating Capability

         The generating capability figures used for each period are obtained by multiplying the
seasonal capabilities by an availability factor, which is based on the period, unit location, and
NERC Generating Availability Data Systems (GADS) category of the unit. Data from 2020
through 2024 were used because those were the latest available on the NERC web site as of
August 2026. The GADS database provides national average operating information for
generating units by unit type and size range. For example, it provides data for coal-fired steam
units with capacities between 300 MW and 399 MW.

         For each period and each generating unit, the availability factor adjusts for the
following.

    a) Unplanned outage rates by GADS category
         For a given GADS category, the study assumes that unplanned (forced) outage rates
(as a share of generating capability available after allowing for planned outages) are constant
across seasons and generating units, regardless of owner. Based on GADS data for 2020-2024,
the study calculates an equivalent forced outage rate (EIFOR), which measures the share of
generating capability in a GADS category that is not available because of forced outages. The
computation is EIFOR = (FOH)/AH, where FOH is number of forced outage hours and AH is
total hours available for generation after planned outages (but before forced outages). 5

        As specified by the Commission, the study generally uses ceiling prices for
transmission service from Schedules 1, 2 and 8 of the utility’s pro forma open-access

        When tariffs are available, we calculate rates for off-peak, peak and spike categories.
Because of discounting and the nature of baseload purchases, off-peak rates are often lower

calculate hourly off-peak rates, we divide the weekly rate by 168, the number of hours in a

hourly rates in its tariff, we use the maximum tariff rates. Step 2: When a utility does not post
off-peak hourly rates, we calculate a peak rate based on other tariff information. To calculate
hourly peak rates, we divide the weekly rate by 80—the “Appalachian” method.
